title: Three stops with no breath, long ii, and where a syllable dies

slides.heading: Three letters, one vowel, two rules
body: Three consonants, one long vowel, two rules.
The three are alike enough that one of them teaches the others.
Last lesson's letters let sounds ring on. These stop them.

slides.heading: One district, and no breath in any of it
body: All three are mid class, and mid class is the market.
The air stops, and no breath follows it.
English blows air on key and pin. Your palm stays still on these three.

slides.heading: The pen, before anything else
body: Real paper, a real pen, still in front of you.
This is the first thing people quietly stop doing.
Go and fetch them if they have wandered off.

slides.heading: The first of the three
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means *chicken*.
Flatter than an English g, and no breath behind it.

slides.heading: The stall that opens first
body: She opens the corner stall before anyone else arrives.
Her son sleeps under the stall while she works. Remember him.
The chicken eats the spilled grain, and the rats stay away.

slides.heading: The bird that stopped crowing
body: A year of glorious golden grain, and it stopped crowing.
What is left is a cluck: short, flat, no breath, over at once.
No circle, an open frame, and a beak arching left.

slides.heading: The chicken's letter
body: No circle anywhere on it.
An open frame, and one beak-line arching to the left.

slides.heading: Write it before you meet the next one
body: **Headless.** No loop, so the head rule does not apply here.
The beak arches left. Nothing curls.
Say both halves of its name **out loud**, every time.

slides.heading: The second of the three
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means *child*.
A plain flat d, with nothing blown out behind it.

slides.heading: Drowsy, dreaming, deep in the dark
body: The same small son from the chicken's stall. This is where he sleeps.
Drowsy, dreaming, deep in the dark under the stall.
Curled up, one arm under his head, toes over the edge.
The whole row minds that bowl, loudly, at anyone who forgets.

slides.heading: How a market learns to be quiet
body: The row trades quietly, and the quiet sounds are today's three.
Each one stops the air and releases nothing.
A bowl, a head curled inside, and a point at the bottom.

slides.heading: The child's letter
body: A bowl with a smooth rim, head curled inside.
Drawn down to a point at the bottom.

slides.heading: Now this one, the same way
body: **Start at the head**, curled inside the bowl, clockwise.
Out into the bowl, down to the point at the bottom.
Out loud, every time, while the hand is moving.

slides.heading: The third of the three
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means *leaf*.
Lips together, sound, stop. No breath.

slides.heading: The leaf that got out of hand
body: One big, bright, beautiful leaf out of an open bucket.
One leaf the size of a door, and the only shade the corner stall has.
An open bucket, straight-walled and flat-bottomed, with something growing out of it.

slides.heading: The leaf's letter
body: An open bucket: straight walls, flat bottom.
The child's letter curves to a point. This one runs flat across the bottom.

slides.heading: And the third, which you half know already
body: **Start at the head**, top left, clockwise.
Straight down, flat across, straight up. Walls level.
Write it beside the child's letter and compare the two bottoms.

slides.prompt: Say the three letters' sounds with a palm held close to your lips. What should you feel, and what would feeling something tell you?

answers: Nothing should move. These three release no breath.
A moving hand means you said the English sound.
Thai keeps the breathy ones as separate letters, so it changes the word.

slides.heading: Back to the house
body: One house, and the room is decided by where the vowel is written.
Lesson one's vowel is written after, so it is in the back yard.
Today's is written above. That is the roof.

slides.heading: The lodger on the roof
body: The name begins with the vowel it stands for. Everyone here is named that way.
The word means *more*.
Written above the consonant, so he lives on the roof.
Whole word, ordinary. First syllable alone in front of a name, an insult.

slides.heading: The mark itself
body: It rides above the consonant like a beret.
The brim flicks up at the right edge. Next lesson says what it is for.

slides.heading: Write the vowel too
body: It is never written alone. Always above a consonant.
Put it over letters you already know.
Say the **whole syllable** out loud, the sound the marks make together.

slides.heading: Two words you can already read
body: Two words, both built from letters you have.
**Say both out loud first.**

slides.heading: Those two
body: **มี** — to have, or *there is*.
**ดี** — good.

slides.heading: Where a syllable stops dead
body: The harbour's letters let a syllable ring on. These three seal it.
A syllable sealed like that is *dead*. One that can ring on is *live*.
The ending decides it, whatever letter opens the syllable.

slides.heading: Mid class, live syllable
body: A mid class letter on a live syllable lands flat.
So does a low class one. For now the two agree.
They come apart as soon as a syllable ends dead.

slides.prompt: One of the two words you read earlier ends live and the other ends dead. Which is which, and what exactly makes the difference?

answers: Live: it ends on a long vowel with nothing after it.
Dead: the chicken's letter seals it and the sound stops.
Same letter at the front. The ending is what decides.

slides.heading: Three words, and no new letters
body: Read each one before the answer comes.
Everything here is from lessons one to three.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: The leaf's letter, a long vowel, and a hum to close it.
**Say it aloud before you turn this over.**

slides.heading: That one
body: **บาง** — thin, or *some*.

slides.heading: And this one
body: The mouse's letter, then the chicken's letter sealing it.
**Out loud, before you turn it over.**

slides.heading: That one
body: **นก** — a bird. Short, stopped, over at once.

slides.heading: One more
body: The child's letter, with today's vowel on the roof.

slides.heading: And that one
body: **ดี** — good.

slides.heading: Three lessons in
body: Two districts: the harbour rings on, the market stops.
Eight letters, two vowels, one room of the house open.
Next: the shortener, and the shortcut it gives you.
